question: A procurement officer pasted a sixty-page supplier contract into Claude and asked for a summary of the commercial terms. Which two evaluation steps should she take before circulating it? Select two.
options: A) Accept it if it reads coherently from beginning to end without any obvious contradiction.
B) Ask Claude whether its summary is accurate and treat a confident yes as confirmation.
C) Take the precise contractual vocabulary in the summary as a sign of a careful reading.
D) Open the contract and read the clauses behind several of the summarised commercial points.
E) List the terms she needed covered and check whether any of them are simply absent.
correct_answers: D) Open the contract and read the clauses behind several of the summarised commercial points.
E) List the terms she needed covered and check whether any of them are simply absent.
explanations: Coherence is a property of the writing. A fluent summary of the wrong clauses reads exactly as smoothly as a fluent summary of the right ones.
A self-assessment is generated the same way the summary was. Claude cannot independently confirm its own reading of the contract, so this adds no evidence.
Precise legal vocabulary is easy to produce and is not evidence of fidelity. Confident phrasing is a common feature of inaccurate summaries.
Correct. Spot-checking against the source is the only way to catch a term that has been subtly restated, such as a notice period reported as thirty rather than ninety days.
Correct. Checking for omissions is a different test from checking what is present: a summary can be entirely accurate and still leave out the termination terms.
